judge_assessment.explanation: The mathematics is exactly as the judge reports. I re-modelled all eight stories: 6−2=4 crayons, 9−4=5 stickers, 7−4=3 more red cubes, 8−3=5 grapes, 9−5=4 fewer ducks, 10−□=6 giving 4 buttons, □+3=9 giving 6 shells, and the challenge 8−3=5 apples then 5−2=3 more apples than pears. verify.json matches item for item, the take-from and comparison structures are correctly distinguished (the key's 'the matched pairs are removed from the bigger group in thought, not in fact' is a genuinely correct account of why subtraction answers a comparison), and every story states its units. What the judge did not check is what the child is asked to WRITE. Problems 3, 4, 5 and 8 each ask for the subtraction equation as well as the number ('Write the subtraction that answers the question'; 'write the subtraction equation and answer'; 'Write both subtraction equations'), and every one of those problems carries a single verify entry for the numeric result only. Problems 4, 5 and 7 additionally require a drawn and marked representation ('Draw the grapes as dots. Cross out the ones Leo eats'; 'Draw Sam's shells, circle the 3 extra ones') with no manual entry anywhere in the file, while final_response.md states 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — every answer on both documents is machine-verified.'

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 5's key entry names the symmetry that comparison stories turn on: 'Same gap, two sentences: there are 4 fewer ducks than frogs, and also 4 more frogs than ducks. Both describe the same matching.' Asking the 'fewer' direction and then showing it is the same difference is exactly the distinction K/1 comparison work usually skips.

Problem 8 is a real two-step challenge and the key guards its trap explicitly: 'Part (b) ... uses the answer from part (a) rather than the starting 8 ... comparing the pears with the original 8 apples gives 6 and ignores the eating. Finish step one, write its answer down, and only then start step two.'

Units are carried into every boxed answer ('4 crayons', '3 more red cubes', '4 fewer ducks', '5 apples') and the worksheet header teaches it as a rule ('Always say the unit out loud with your answer: not just "four", but "four crayons"'), which is precisely the 'state units explicitly' the prompt asked for.

The two missing-part items are placed adjacently but on opposite sides of the operation — problem 6 hides the CHANGE (10 − □ = 6) and problem 7 hides the SMALLER GROUP (□ + 3 = 9) — so the child cannot pattern-match a procedure across them.

root_causes.description: Half the sheet prints two responses and verifies one. Problems 3, 4 and 5 ask for the subtraction equation AND the answer; problem 8 asks for 'both subtraction equations' plus the two results. verify.json gives problems 3, 4 and 5 a single eval each and problem 8 two evals for the two values, so the equation the child writes — which is where a take-from/comparison confusion would actually show up — is never checked. scripts/verify.py's coverage gate is satisfied by one entry per problem id, so this passes silently.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-028/worksheet.pdf problem 4: 'Then write the subtraction equation and answer: how many grapes are still on the plate?' — verify.json id 4 is one eval, expected 5.
worksheet.pdf problem 3: 'How many more red cubes than blue cubes are there? Write the subtraction that answers the question.' — verify.json id 3 is one eval, expected 3.
worksheet.pdf problem 8(b): 'Write both subtraction equations.' — verify.json id 8 holds two evals (5 and 3), the values only.
scripts/verify.py coverage gate: 'Every worksheet problem needs at least one check (use type manual if unverifiable)' — id-level, so a second printed response is invisible to the build.

root_causes.description: Three problems require a drawn and marked representation that is recorded as fully machine-verified. Problem 4 asks the child to draw eight grapes and cross out three, problem 5 to draw two matched rows of frogs and ducks, problem 7 to draw Sam's nine shells and circle the three extra. The drawing is not decorative here — the answer key grades it ('Draw 8 dots for the grapes, then cross out 3'; 'Draw Sam's 9 shells, circle the 3 extra') — yet each problem carries only a numeric entry, no manual entry exists in the file, and the delivery message states that everything is machine-verified.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 7: 'Draw Sam's shells, circle the 3 extra ones, and count what is left.' — verify.json id 7 is {'type': 'solve', 'expected': [6]} and nothing else.
worksheet.pdf problems 4 and 5 similarly instruct 'Draw the grapes as dots. Cross out the ones Leo eats.' and 'Draw a row of frogs and a row of ducks, one under the other, and match them up.'

evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-028/final_response.md: 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — every answer on both documents is machine-verified.'; the packet's machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags false.
SKILL.md line 257 lists 'word problem setups' and 'constructions' among the cases that must be declared manual.

improvements.title: Coverage gate must count printed answer slots, not problem ids
improvements.proposed_change: scripts/verify.py's coverage gate currently only requires that every id in 1..problem_count has at least one check (see the 'Coverage gap' block near line 2015), which is why a problem printing two blanks passes with one entry. Add a slot-count gate: have tests/check_answer_line.py (it already segments the worksheet .tex by problem via _tex_segments) count the response slots inside each problem's span — \ansblank, \answerline/\ansline, standalone \underline{\hspace{...}} blanks, and lettered parts '(a)'/'(b)' — and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying that id, naming the uncovered slot. Allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field ("slots": N) for the case where two blanks genuinely hold one answer (a restated equation), so the gate is precise rather than merely noisy. State the rule in SKILL.md beside the existing coverage paragraph: one verify entry per printed response, not per problem number. In this case the uncovered slots are the written subtraction equations in problems 3, 4, 5 and 8 — the place where a take-from / comparison confusion would actually be visible — which the key supplies but no verify entry covers.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet .tex with a single problem printing '$10 + \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$' and a verify JSON with one eval entry for that id; assert the answer-line gate exits non-zero and names problem 1's second slot. Add the missing entry and assert exit 0. Today the gate passes both, so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the single largest verification blind spot in the run: any answer the child actually writes down is either machine-checked or explicitly declared manual, and the answer key's bank stops being narrower than the worksheet.
improvements.risk: Medium. Slot detection is heuristic over LaTeX, so it can false-fail sheets that print a blank as scaffolding (a restated equation, a cross-out target). The "slots" opt-out and a fixture suite covering the \ansblank, \answerline and lettered-part shapes keep the false positives bounded; ship the gate as exit 2 (manual review) for one run before making it exit 1 if that risk is judged too high.

improvements.title: An explanation or drawn/marked response must carry a manual verify entry
improvements.proposed_change: SKILL.md already says to reserve 'manual' for genuinely open reasoning and to use it for 'any explanation/reasoning answer', but nothing enforces it, so the instruction loses to the convenience of a single numeric entry. Add a gate (natural home: tests/check_answer_line.py, which already has the per-problem .tex spans) that scans each problem's student-facing prose for open-response imperatives — 'explain', 'tell what ... did wrong', 'show how you know', 'draw', 'circle', 'cross out', 'mark', 'match ... with a line' — and fails when that problem has no entry of type 'manual'. The numeric check stays; the manual entry is ADDED alongside it so the drawn or spoken part is routed to a human instead of being silently counted as verified. In this case the triggers are the drawn-and-marked responses in problems 4 ('Draw the grapes as dots. Cross out the ones Leo eats'), 5 ('Draw a row of frogs and a row of ducks ... and match them up') and 7 ('Draw Sam's shells, circle the 3 extra ones'). The numeric checks stay; a manual entry is ADDED so the drawn model the key grades is routed to a human rather than counted as verified.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet problem whose text is 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times. Then write the right answer.' paired with a verify JSON holding only an eval entry for that id: assert the gate exits non-zero and names the open-response phrase. Add {'id':N,'type':'manual','desc':...} and assert exit 0 with the run reporting manual-review items. Today both configurations pass, so the first assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: Gate-chain manual flags start telling the truth, final_response.md stops claiming 'nothing is flagged for manual review' on sheets that contain an explanation prompt, and the human reviewer is pointed at exactly the items a machine cannot judge.
improvements.risk: Medium. Keyword scanning over child-facing prose will catch incidental uses ('circle the greater number', where the circle is the same answer as the verified value). Mitigate by requiring the phrase to introduce a response the key grades separately, and by allowing an explicit '"open": false' acknowledgement on the entry so authors can dismiss a false positive deliberately rather than by accident.

case_summary: Mathematically exact and pedagogically careful — the take-from / comparison distinction is drawn correctly and defended in the key, units are carried into every answer as the prompt required, the two missing-part items hide different positions, and the two-step challenge explicitly guards against comparing the pears with the original count. All eight answers (4, 5, 3, 5, 4, 4, 6, and 5 then 3) check out. The defects are in what the verification claims to cover. Four problems ask the child to write the subtraction equation alongside the number, and only the number is checked — which is the wrong half, since a child who models a comparison as an addition would produce the right difference through the wrong equation. Three problems require a drawing that the answer key explicitly grades, with no manual entry declared, while final_response.md tells the reader that every answer on both documents is machine-verified. None of this is caught by the build, because the coverage gate asks only for one check per problem number.
